title.text: Language models: tokens, attention and next-word probability

objects.text: How does a language model turn your words into an answer, and why can the same question give different answers?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 5 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 5. Last time, in Session 4, you saw that a vector is a list of numbers, that the dot product multiplies matching numbers and adds them, and that an embedding is a vector placing a text so that similar meanings sit close. Today you see what a language model does with numbers like those to produce an answer.

I use a real open model, GPT-2, running on this laptop, so every real figure on the slides is a recorded result.

You will have computed a softmax, a temperature and a small self-attention yourself, with three numbers. And you will be able to explain two things colleagues ask: why the same question gives different answers, and why a confident answer can be wrong.

title.text:
Your two hours: most of
the time is your own work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_ed891596.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You watch a real open model work, then compute its core step with a pencil.

slides.notes:
To get there we have two hours. Today has more maths than usual, so the ideas take fifty-five minutes, and I build every formula slowly from numbers you can check with a pencil: tokens, scores, the number e, softmax, temperature, the loss used in training, and self-attention. Every real figure comes from an open model I ran on a laptop.

Then I run it live for fifteen minutes. After the break you work a softmax by hand for twenty minutes, and we end by deciding where this behaviour helps or hurts in your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is a vector?
2.  How do you compute a dot product?
3.  What is an embedding?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 4. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is a vector? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A list of numbers, such as two film ratings (3, 4). Each position in the list is a dimension.

Question two. How do you compute a dot product? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Multiply the matching numbers of two vectors and add the results. A bigger dot product means the vectors agree more.

Question three. What is an embedding? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. A vector, produced by a trained model, that places a text so that similar meanings sit close together.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text:
How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_225326ec.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold the training loop from Session 0, neurons and layers from Session 1 and vectors, dot product, embeddings from Session 4. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: tokens, logits, softmax, next-token loss, attention.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 6: what happens when this is done at huge scale. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A token is a piece of text the model reads. Its token id is its number in the fixed vocabulary.
The raw score the model gives each possible next token. Higher means more likely.
Turns the scores into probabilities: e to each score, divided by the total.
Sampling draws the next token by chance. Temperature divides the scores first: low sharpens, high flattens.
Each token weighs the earlier tokens, using a query, a key and a value.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Token, token id. A token is a piece of text the model reads. Its token id is its number in the fixed vocabulary.

Logit. The raw score the model gives each possible next token. Higher means more likely.

Softmax. Turns the scores into probabilities: e to each score, divided by the total.

Temperature, sampling. Sampling draws the next token by chance. Temperature divides the scores first: low sharpens, high flattens.

Self-attention. Each token weighs the earlier tokens, using a query, a key and a value.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
Ask the same model the same question
twice and the answers can differ

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_two_runs_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Ask the same model the same question twice and the answers can differ

objects.text: Two real runs of GPT-2, an open model, with the same words in.

slides.notes:
Here is the first idea, and it starts with a puzzle every executive has noticed. You ask an assistant the same question twice and get two different answers. I gave an open model, GPT-2, the same eight words twice. An open model is one whose trained numbers are published, so I can run it on this laptop.

One run says the delivery was delayed. The other says it was fast and the service was excellent. Nobody changed anything. By the end of the ideas you can explain why, step by step. Where do we start? With what the machine actually reads.

title.text:
A tokenizer cuts text into tokens:
words, parts of words or punctuation

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_tokens_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A tokenizer cuts text into tokens: words, parts of words or punctuation

objects.text: A token is a piece of text the model reads. The tokenizer is the program that cuts text into tokens.

runs.text: Common words are one token.
Names, numbers and rare words split into several.

slides.notes:
So what does the machine actually read?

Neither letters nor whole sentences. It reads tokens. A token is a piece of text, and the tokenizer is the program that cuts text into tokens. Here is a real sentence, Nile Valley Foods delivers maize flour to Mbale, cut by the real GPT-2 tokenizer. Common words such as flour or delivers are one token.

Nile becomes N and ile, and Mbale becomes Mb and ale. As an analogy, think of syllables, though the cuts come from how often pieces of text appear in training text, and they do not follow syllables. Eight words became eleven tokens, and the invoice line below splits into eighteen.

The machine still needs numbers, though, so how does a token become one?

title.text:
Each token has a token id: its number
in a fixed vocabulary of 50,257

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_token_ids_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Each token has a token id: its number in a fixed vocabulary of 50,257

objects.text: Real GPT-2 tokens and token ids for the same sentence, recorded 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
Every token gets a number. The vocabulary is the fixed list of every token the model knows, 50,257 of them for GPT-2, made once before training. The token id is the place of a token in that list, like a product code in a shop catalogue. So the sentence you just saw becomes eleven numbers: N is 45, ile is 576, Valley is 6,916, and so on to the full stop, which is 13.

Most tokens carry the space in front of the word, so space Valley is one token. From here on the model only sees these ids. Later today we see how each id turns into a whole row of numbers.

title.text:
Amounts, names and Swahili need
more tokens than plain English

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_token_counts_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Amounts, names and Swahili need more tokens than plain English

objects.text: Real GPT-2 token counts. A second tokenizer program, tiktoken, gave the same tokens.

slides.notes:
Does the number of tokens matter for your work?

Here is the evidence. Five sentences, counted two ways: the grey bar is words, the gold bar is tokens. The invoice sentence has seven words but eighteen tokens, because the amount and the invoice number split into small tokens. The Swahili order has five words and fourteen tokens.

This matters in two ways. Providers set prices and limits in tokens, and the context window, the most tokens a model can read at once, is also counted in tokens: 1,024 for GPT-2. And a model handles rare tokens less well, because it saw them less in training.

Now, what does the model do with these ids?

title.text:
Next-token prediction works like phone
autocomplete, repeated again and again

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_next_loop_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Next-token prediction works like phone autocomplete, repeated again and again

objects.text: Your keyboard suggests a few words. A language model scores every token, picks one, adds it and repeats.

runs.text: The longer text goes back in for the next token.
Nothing in the loop looks facts up.

slides.notes:
It does one thing only, and you already know a small version of it. Your phone keyboard suggests the next word as you type, and you tap one. On the left are the three most likely next tokens GPT-2 gave after Thank you for your: support at thirty percent, continued at ten and patience at five.

A real keyboard uses its own method, so read this as the same idea. A language model does next-token prediction. It gives a score to every one of its 50,257 tokens, one token is picked, it joins the text, and the longer text goes round again. Those scores are the heart of it, so let me show you real ones.

title.text:
The model gives every possible
next token a score, called a logit

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_logits_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The model gives every possible next token a score, called a logit

objects.text: A logit is a raw score, one for each of the 50,257 tokens. A higher score means more likely.

runs.text: Scores can be any number, even negative.
Only which is higher, and by how much, matters.
Scores are hard to read: we want percentages.

slides.notes:
These are the real scores GPT-2 gave after Please pay the invoice within thirty. The industry name for such a raw score is a logit. The last step of the model produces one logit for every token in the vocabulary, and later today we open the model to see where they come from.

An opening bracket scores minus 20.70, days minus 22.06, a hyphen minus 22.62. The lowest of all fifty thousand is minus 55.93. The GPT-2 scores happen to be negative; that is fine, because only the order and the gaps matter. The bracket beats days by 1.36 points. But what does 1.36 points mean in percent?

Scores do not say. To turn them into percentages we need one small piece of maths, the number e.

title.text:
The number e is about 2.72, and e to the
x means multiplying e by itself x times

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_exp_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The number e is about 2.72, and e to the x means multiplying e by itself x times

objects.text: e = 2.718... is a fixed number. e to the x, written eˣ, multiplies e by itself x times.

runs.text: e to the 2 = e × e = 7.39.
e to the 0 = 1. e to the minus 1 = 1 ÷ e = 0.37.
A calculator has an eˣ key; spreadsheets use EXP.

slides.notes:
You met e for a moment in Session 4, inside the log of TF-IDF. Like the 3.14 that belongs to every circle, e is a fixed number that turns up throughout mathematics: 2.718 and on, about 2.72. E to the x, written as e with a small x raised, means multiply e by itself x times.

E to the one is 2.72. E to the two is e times e, 7.39. E to the three is 20.09. E to the zero is one, by definition. A negative power means divide: e to the minus one is one divided by e, 0.37. On a calculator use the e to the x key, and in a spreadsheet the EXP function.

On the curve, it never drops below zero and climbs faster and faster. Both facts are exactly why the model uses it.

title.text:
Why take e to each score: every
result is positive, and the gaps stretch

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_why_exp_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Why take e to each score: every result is positive, and the gaps stretch

objects.text: After e, every number is positive and each extra point multiplies it by 2.72.

slides.notes:
Why not simply divide each score by the total, the way you work out a share of a budget?

Try it on scores minus one, zero and one. The total is zero, and you cannot divide by zero; and a share of minus one makes no sense. Now take e to each score first: 0.37, 1 and 2.72. Every number is now above zero, so shares will work.

And the gaps stretch: each extra point of score makes the number 2.72 times bigger, so a clearly higher score earns a clearly bigger share. Those are the two reasons. Now we can turn scores into probabilities, with three easy numbers.

title.text:
Softmax by hand: e to each score,
add them up, divide each by the total

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_softmax_steps_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Softmax by hand: e to each score, add them up, divide each by the total

objects.text: Illustrative scores 2, 1 and 0, chosen for easy arithmetic.

slides.notes:
Let me do it with a pencil. Say the model scores days 2, weeks 1 and minutes 0; I chose these for easy arithmetic. Step one, e to each score: 7.39, 2.72 and 1.00, from the table you just saw. Step two, add them up: 7.39 plus 2.72 plus 1.00 is 11.11.

Step three, divide each by the total: 7.39 divided by 11.11 is 0.665, then 0.245 and 0.090. A probability is a share between zero and one, so 0.665 is 66.5 percent, about two chances in three. Together they make 100 percent, always. This recipe has a name, softmax, and here it is written as a formula.

title.text:
The softmax formula: the same
three steps, written with symbols

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_softmax_formula_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The softmax formula: the same three steps, written with symbols

objects.text: Softmax turns scores into probabilities between 0 and 1 that add up to 1.

runs.text: The highest score gets the biggest share.
Adding the same amount to every score changes nothing, so negative scores are fine.

slides.notes:
Here are the three steps as the industry writes them. The letters i and j count the tokens: token 1 is days, 2 is weeks, 3 is minutes. Z sub i is the score, the logit, of token i. E to the z sub i is step one.

The large Greek letter sigma means add up, one term for each token j: that is step two, the total. P sub i, the probability of token i, is the division in step three. For days: e to the two, divided by e to the two plus e to the one plus e to the zero, is 7.39 over 11.11, which is 0.665.

One more fact: the scores minus one, zero and one give exactly the same shares as two, one and zero, because only the gaps count. That is why GPT-2 can use negative scores.

title.text:
A real probability distribution: its
shape shows how sure the model is

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_next_three_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A real probability distribution: its shape shows how sure the model is

objects.text: Real GPT-2 probabilities after softmax over all 50,257 tokens. Top six shown.

slides.notes:
The full list of probabilities over every token is called a probability distribution. Here are three real ones. After please pay the invoice within thirty, softmax of those real scores puts sixty-nine percent on an opening bracket and eighteen on days. Few good choices. After the customer was angry because the delivery was, the choices are many and close: delayed, not, late.

After Nile Valley Foods is a food distributor based in, the model has no idea and spreads its bets across American places. The real answer, Jinja, is not on the list, yet a fluent sentence still comes out. The probabilities describe likely text; nothing in them checks facts.

So how is one token chosen from such a list?

title.text:
Sampling draws the next token by
chance, in proportion to its probability

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_raffle_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Sampling draws the next token by chance, in proportion to its probability

objects.text: Sampling is like drawing one ticket from a hat: 67 tickets say days, 24 weeks, 9 minutes.

runs.text: Days comes out about two times in three.
Greedy decoding always takes the top token.
This is why the same question can give different answers.

slides.notes:
There are two standard ways to choose. Sampling means drawing the next token at random, in proportion to its probability. Picture our softmax answer as a hat with one hundred tickets: sixty-seven say days, twenty-four say weeks and nine say minutes. Draw one. Usually you get days, sometimes weeks, now and then minutes.

Greedy decoding is the other way: always take the token with the highest probability, so always days. Most chat assistants sample, and each drawn token changes everything that follows. That is the answer to our opening puzzle. There is also a setting that changes the odds in the hat before you draw, called temperature.

title.text:
Temperature divides every score by T before
softmax: the same numbers, recomputed

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_temp_steps_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Temperature divides every score by T before softmax: the same numbers, recomputed

objects.text: Same illustrative scores 2, 1, 0. Percentages rounded to one decimal.

slides.notes:
Temperature, written T, is one number you divide every score by, before softmax. Take T equals two. Step one, divide: the scores 2, 1 and 0 become 1, 0.5 and 0. Step two, e to each: 2.72, 1.65 and 1.00. Step three, divide by their total, 5.37: days 50.6 percent, weeks 30.7, minutes 18.6.

At temperature one we had 66.5 percent for days, so a higher temperature flattens the odds. A temperature of 0.5 doubles the scores to 4, 2 and 0, and days jumps to 86.7 percent: a lower temperature sharpens. Dividing by T shrinks or widens the gaps between the scores, and you saw that the gaps are all that matter.

title.text:
On real GPT-2 scores, low temperature
sharpens and high temperature flattens

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_temp_bars_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: On real GPT-2 scores, low temperature sharpens and high temperature flattens

objects.text: Real GPT-2 logits divided by the temperature T, then softmax.

slides.notes:
Here is the same recipe on the real scores after the customer was angry because the delivery was. At temperature 0.2, delayed takes seventy-eight percent and the rest nearly vanish. At one, the probabilities are as trained: delayed has eleven percent, and sixty-seven percent sits outside the top five.

At 1.8 the distribution flattens, and ninety-six percent sits outside the top five, spread over thousands of unlikely tokens. The formula at the bottom is the softmax formula from before, with each score z divided by T inside the power. Low temperature gives repeatable answers. High temperature gives variety and eventually nonsense. Let me show you what that looks like in words.

title.text:
Sampled text: low temperature repeats,
high temperature drifts into noise

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_temp_samples_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Sampled text: low temperature repeats, high temperature drifts into noise

objects.text: Real sampled completions, three of six per temperature, recorded 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
Percentages are abstract until you read what comes out. I sampled completions from the same prompt at three temperatures. At 0.2, the three runs start the same way, with delayed, and one even repeats itself. At one, the runs go in different directions: a delay, a legal requirement, a rent dispute.

At 1.8 the text is mostly noise. So the opening puzzle has a full answer: the next token is drawn by chance, and temperature sets how adventurous the draw is. Which setting would you want for a contract summary, and which for naming products?

title.text:
Top-k and top-p cut the
probability list before the draw

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_sampling_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Top-k and top-p cut the probability list before the draw

objects.text: Applied to the recorded GPT-2 list after "Please pay the invoice within thirty".

slides.notes:
Two more settings trim the hat before the draw. Read the list from the top. Greedy decoding keeps only the first token. Top-k keeps the k most probable tokens; with k equals two that is the bracket and days. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the fewest top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p.

Read the running total column: 69.3, then 87.1, then 97.3 percent. With p equals 0.9 the total first passes ninety percent at the third token, so three are kept. After the cut, each kept probability is divided by the total of the kept ones, so they add up to one hundred percent again: top-k with k of two gives eighty and twenty percent. I applied these cuts myself to the recorded list.

title.text:
Training uses the Session 0 loop on text: hide
the next token, predict, measure the loss

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_learn_loop_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Training uses the Session 0 loop on text: hide the next token, predict, measure the loss

objects.text: Step 2 shows the trained GPT-2. Early in training the predictions are close to random.

slides.notes:
We have seen how the model uses its scores; now, how did it learn to give good ones?

With the loop from Session 0: predict, measure the loss, adjust, repeat. Take a sentence from a huge body of text, here please pay the invoice within thirty, and hide the next token. The model predicts: bracket sixty-nine percent, days eighteen. The true token is days, so the right answer got only eighteen percent, and the loss should be high.

Gradient descent then nudges the weights so days gets more next time. No person wrote a label: the text holds its own answer, which Session 0 called self-supervised learning. But what number exactly is the loss? That needs one more idea.

title.text:
Next-token loss is minus the log of the
probability given to the right token

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_loss_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Next-token loss is minus the log of the probability given to the right token

objects.text: Loss = minus ln p, where p is the probability the model gave the right token, and ln is the natural logarithm.

runs.text: ln asks: e to what power gives this number? e to the minus 1.71 is 0.18, so ln 0.18 is minus 1.71.
Confident and right costs little; confident and wrong costs a lot.

slides.notes:
We want a loss that is small when the model gave the right token a high probability and large when it gave it a low one. The standard choice is minus the natural logarithm of that probability. The natural logarithm, written ln, undoes e to the x: it asks, e to what power gives this number?

E to the minus 1.71 is 0.18, so ln of 0.18 is minus 1.71, and the minus sign in front makes the loss plus 1.71. Read the curve. Right token at 0.9, confident and right: loss 0.11. At 0.5: loss 0.69. Days at 0.18: 1.71. Right token at 0.01, confident and wrong: 4.61.

The industry name is cross-entropy loss. Over a whole sentence, the probabilities chain together.

title.text:
The probability of a sentence is a chain:
each token given the tokens before it

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_chain_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The probability of a sentence is a chain: each token given the tokens before it

objects.text: Real GPT-2 probabilities for "Thank you for your support", recorded 11 November 2026.

slides.notes:
Here is a real chain. Given the word Thank, GPT-2 gave the token you a probability of 0.0221. Given Thank you, it gave for 0.4271. Given Thank you for, your got 0.2733. Given Thank you for your, support got 0.3035. The bar in the formula reads given. Multiply the four, the way you multiply the chances of several steps that must all happen, each chance taken given the steps before, and the whole continuation gets 0.00078, about eight in ten thousand.

Whole sentences always get tiny numbers, because many choices multiply. So training works with the loss of each step instead: 3.81, 0.85, 1.30 and 1.19, average 1.79. Lowering the average loss over billions of sentences is the whole training goal. Now let us open the model itself, starting where a token id becomes numbers.

title.text:
The embedding matrix is a lookup table:
a token id picks one row of 768 numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_lookup_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The embedding matrix is a lookup table: a token id picks one row of 768 numbers

objects.text: Real GPT-2 sizes and real row 45,458. The other rows are illustrative.

slides.notes:
Inside the model, the first step is a lookup. Recall Session 4: an embedding is a vector, a list of numbers that places a text so that similar meanings sit close. GPT-2 keeps a big table called the embedding matrix, with one row for every token in the vocabulary, 50,257 rows, and each row holds 768 numbers.

The token id picks its row, like finding a line in a phone book by its number. Invoice, with a space in front, is token id 45,458, and its row starts 0.07, minus 0.30, 0.16. Nobody typed these numbers in. They are weights, learned by the same training loop.

One thing is still missing: where the token sits in the sentence.

title.text:
A second table adds position,
because word order changes meaning

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_position_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A second table adds position, because word order changes meaning

objects.text: Real first 4 of 768 numbers: "invoice", 4th token of "Please pay the invoice".

slides.notes:
The dog bit the man and the man bit the dog have the same tokens and opposite meanings, so the model must know the order. GPT-2 keeps a second learned table, the position table, with one row for each place in the text, 1,024 rows, which is why its context window is 1,024 tokens.

The model adds the two rows, number by number. Invoice is the fourth token here: its token row starts 0.0688, the fourth position row starts minus 0.0003, and the sum starts 0.0685. In symbols, x sub t equals E of id sub t plus P of t. T is the position, id sub t the token id at that position, E the token table and P the position table.

This sum, 768 numbers per token, goes into the first block. What happens there?

title.text:
To read "it", the model must look back: one
real GPT-2 head puts 85 percent on "invoice"

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_attn_arrows_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: To read "it", the model must look back: one real GPT-2 head puts 85 percent on "invoice"

objects.text: Self-attention lets each token decide which earlier tokens matter for it. Line thickness shows the share.

runs.text: The shares add up to 100 percent.
A token can only look at earlier tokens.

slides.notes:
Read this sentence: the supplier sent the invoice to the manager because someone needed it. What does it refer to?

You looked back at the earlier words and settled on invoice. A model needs the same skill: the numbers for the token it should carry some of the meaning of invoice. Self-attention is that step. Each token gives every earlier token a share of its attention, the shares add up to one hundred percent, and it blends in their information by those shares.

These are real shares from one part of GPT-2 called an attention head: it gives eighty-five percent to invoice. How does the model work out those shares? An everyday picture first.

title.text:
Query, key and value: in a classroom,
each pupil decides whom to listen to

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_classroom_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Query, key and value: in a classroom, each pupil decides whom to listen to

objects.text: You are Esther and need a red pen. You listen most to the pupil whose key matches your query.

runs.text: Query: what a token is looking for.
Key: what a token offers, to be matched.
Value: the information it hands over.
The percentages are illustrative.

slides.notes:
Imagine you are Esther and you need a red pen, so you ask a question: that is your query. Each earlier pupil holds up a card saying what they have: that is their key. You compare your query with every key and decide how much to listen to each pupil: seventy percent to Brian, who has the red pen.

Then you take what they hand over, which is their value, mostly the red pen from Brian. In the model, every token makes its own query, key and value, each a vector, a list of numbers, made from its embedding by learned weights. The analogy breaks in one place: the model blends a little of every value, while Esther mostly takes one pen. Now the same thing with numbers.

title.text:
Self-attention by hand: score each
key, softmax, then blend the values

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_toy_attention_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Self-attention by hand: score each key, softmax, then blend the values

objects.text: Illustrative numbers. Score, then softmax, then blend the values.

slides.notes:
Here is self-attention with a pencil, with one number for each query, key and value. The token it has the query two. The three earlier tokens have keys 0.5, 1.5 and 1. Step one, score each: query times key, which is the Session 4 dot product with only one number per vector, gives 1, 3 and 2.

Step two, softmax, as you did before: e to each score is 2.72, 20.09 and 7.39, total 30.2, so the weights are nine, sixty-seven and twenty-four percent. Step three, blend the values, the information handed over, which are 2, 6 and 4: 0.09 times 2 plus 0.67 times 6 plus 0.24 times 4 is about 5.2, close to the value of invoice. Now the formula.

title.text:
The attention formula: the same
three steps for every token at once

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_attn_formula_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The attention formula: the same three steps for every token at once

objects.text: Scaled dot-product attention, as written in papers and model cards.

slides.notes:
This is how papers and model cards write it. Q, K and V stack the queries, keys and values, one row per token. K with a small T is K transposed, the key table turned on its side, so that Q times K-transposed, a different T from temperature, computes every query-times-key score at once: a table with one row per token, like the toy scores.

D is how many numbers each key holds, 64 in GPT-2. We divide the scores by the square root of d, the number that times itself gives d, so by eight; this keeps the scores moderate, or softmax would put nearly everything on one token. Softmax turns each row into weights, and times V blends the values.

In our toy, d is one, so dividing changes nothing. Later tokens are blanked out first.

title.text:
The whole real attention table:
block 5, head 4 of GPT-2

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_attn_heat_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The whole real attention table: block 5, head 4 of GPT-2

objects.text: Each row is the softmax row for one token: whom it looks at. Darker red means a larger weight.

runs.text: The empty upper half: later tokens are blanked out.
GPT-2 small runs 12 heads in each of 12 blocks.

slides.notes:
The formula fills a whole table at once, and here is a real one. Each row is one token looking back; each column is an earlier token it may look at; darker red means a larger weight, and each row adds up to one hundred percent. The empty upper half is the blanking you just saw: a token cannot look at tokens that come later.

The bottom row, circled, is the token it, with eighty-five percent on invoice. An attention head is one such calculation with its own learned queries, keys and values. GPT-2 small runs twelve heads side by side in each of its twelve blocks, which I explain next. One head shows one pattern.

How typical is this tidy one?

title.text:
Most heads do something else,
and I searched for this one

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_head_grid_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Most heads do something else, and I searched for this one

objects.text: Of 144 heads, 78 put over half their attention on the first token. Only one put over 30 percent on "invoice".

runs.text: I searched all 144 to find a head that shows a clear pattern.

slides.notes:
Not very typical, and here I show the search itself. Each small square is one head, laid out by block and head number. On the left, the darker the square, the more the token it rests on the first token of the sentence. Seventy-eight of the one hundred and forty-four heads do that, a pattern researchers often describe as a resting place; I did not verify why.

On the right, only one head, ringed, puts much attention on invoice. I found it by searching. So a neat attention picture is a selected example. Treat anyone who says the model attends to the right thing with caution unless they show you the search. Attention is half of a block; here is the other half.

title.text:
A transformer block is self-attention plus
the neurons of Session 1; GPT-2 stacks 12

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_block_peek_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A transformer block is self-attention plus the neurons of Session 1; GPT-2 stacks 12

objects.text: Real GPT-2 sizes. Simplified: layer normalisation and residual connections left out.

slides.notes:
Here is one transformer block opened up. In come 768 numbers per token, the sums you saw from the two tables. First, self-attention blends in information from earlier tokens. Then comes the feed-forward network, and these are the neurons of Session 1: a hidden layer of 3,072 neurons, each taking a weighted sum of the 768 numbers, adding a bias and applying an activation function, then an output layer that brings it back to 768 numbers.

Out go 768 numbers per token, now enriched. One block holds 7,087,872 parameters, the weights and biases. I leave out two small steps: layer normalisation rescales the numbers, and a residual connection adds the input of each part back to its output. GPT-2 small stacks twelve blocks, each feeding the next. Let me put the whole machine together.

title.text:
Put together: tokens, embeddings, 12
transformer blocks, logits, probabilities

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t05_stack_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Put together: tokens, embeddings, 12 transformer blocks, logits, probabilities

objects.text: GPT-2 small stacks 12 transformer blocks, then scores all 50,257 tokens.

runs.text: It has 124 million parameters, all set by the training loop.
Its context window is 1,024 tokens.

slides.notes:
You now have every part, so here is the whole machine top to bottom. The tokenizer cuts text into tokens with ids. Each id picks a row of the embedding matrix, plus its position row. The numbers pass through twelve transformer blocks. At the end, the numbers of the last token are compared with every token row to give 50,257 logits, the scores we started from, and softmax makes a probability distribution.

One token is picked by sampling, and the loop repeats. GPT-2 small has one hundred and twenty-four million parameters, all set by the training loop, and a context window of 1,024 tokens. Modern assistants are far larger, but the loop is the same. Everything so far was recorded, so now I run it live.

title.text:
Demonstration: a real model,
run live on this laptop

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_a905c1a1.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: a real model, run live on this laptop

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: The token count compared with the word count.
The shape of each distribution: tall or flat.
Same prompt, different completions.
Your sentence from your own work.

slides.notes:
You have seen the recorded numbers; now I run the same kind of thing live, for about fifteen minutes. It is GPT-2 small, running on this laptop with no internet. First I type a sentence and show its tokens. Then I show the top ten next tokens with their probabilities, the softmax of the scores.

Then I sample the same prompt at low, normal and high temperature. Watch the token count against the word count, and the shape of each distribution, tall or flat. Then give me a sentence from your own work, such as a clause or an invoice line, and we look at its tokens together.

The recorded numbers on these slides are the fallback if the laptop misbehaves.

title.text: Work a softmax and a temperature by hand

objects.text: 20 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Turn three scores into probabilities, then see what a higher temperature does.

runs.text: e to each score: 3, 2 and 0.
Add the three. Divide each by the total.
Divide the scores by T = 2 first. Repeat.
Say which temperature gives the safer answer.
Extra: if weeks was right, loss = −ln of its probability.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_112b5d47.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: The worksheet with both sets of probabilities and one sentence on what you see.

slides.notes:
What did you notice in the live run, tall or flat distributions, and how did the token count compare with the word count?

Now you work the same arithmetic yourself, for twenty minutes, with a calculator or a spreadsheet, and I walk round. The worksheet has three scores: 3, 2 and 0. Take e to each score, add the three, then divide each by the total. The table shows the finished first half.

Then divide the scores by two, a temperature of two, and repeat; expect about fifty-five, thirty-three and twelve percent. Which temperature gives the safer answer, and which gives more variety?

If you finish early, say the right token was weeks and work out its loss, minus ln of its probability. Call me over when you have both sets.

title.text:
Where would you let next-token
prediction help or hurt in your work?

objects.text: Pick one real task from your job. Is next-token prediction the right engine for it?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.80.png
objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Draft
Variety is welcome. A person edits the result.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png
objects.alt: check

objects.text: Draft and check
Useful, but every fact or figure is checked against a source.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.80.png
objects.alt: folder

objects.text: Needs a source
The answer must come from your documents. Wait for Session 9.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.80.png
objects.alt: shield

objects.text: Keep it human
Exact wording or amounts matter too much for a likely guess.
Write the task, your choice and one reason in your workbook.

slides.notes:
Your worksheet showed that a low temperature repeats and a high one varies, and that the model only ever produces likely text. Take one real task from your job. Is next-token prediction the right engine for it?

Draft means variety is welcome and a person edits, such as a customer reply or product names. Draft and check means it is useful, but every fact and figure is checked against a source, such as a CV summary. Needs a source means the answer must come from your own documents, and Session 9 shows how.

Keep it human means exact wording or amounts matter too much for a likely guess, such as reconciling amounts. Tell me your task, your choice and one reason.

title.text:
Keep the one-page sheet: how a
language model chooses its next token

objects.text: What you keep from today

You have chosen where next-token prediction fits your work, and you take the whole session home on one page. The sheet has tokens, scores, e and softmax, temperature, top-k and top-p, the next-token loss, query, key and value, and five questions to ask about any language-model answer. Keep it beside your keyboard.
